references.text: The Lord says that the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and their sin is very grave, and that he will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to him
Abraham asks the Lord to spare the city if there are ten righteous people there, and the Lord says he will spare it for the sake of the ten righteous
The angels warn Lot about the coming destruction and help him and his family flee from the city
Moses describes a land devastated by sulfur and salt, like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, as a warning to Israel
Isaiah says that if the Lord had not left a small remnant, Israel would have become like Sodom and been like Gomorrah
Isaiah prophesies that Babylon will be like when God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah
Jeremiah prophesies that Babylon will be like when God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, without inhabitants
Ezekiel mentions Sodom's sins as pride, abundance, and failure to help the poor and needy
Amos says that God overthrew some of them just as he overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, a direct reference to their destruction
Jesus says it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Sodom than for the city that rejects his disciples
Jesus compares the day of his return to the day when Lot left Sodom, when fire and sulfur rained down from heaven
Peter uses God's judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah, which were reduced to ashes, as an example of what awaits the ungodly
Jude mentions Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire
The psalm's description of heavenly judgment with fire and hail serves as a theological parallel to God's judgment on Sodom.
Both texts illustrate God's judgment through fire falling directly down from heaven.
Peter interprets the event theologically as a warning for those who live ungodly lives.
Revelation uses fire and sulfur as a direct image of final judgment, drawn from the destruction of Sodom.
